title: Interfaces (contracts with default methods)
hook: An interface is a contract — a list of members that a class or struct promises to provide. Unlike a base class, you can implement many interfaces, which is how C# adds extra capabilities without using up your single inheritance slot.

blocks.text: An **interface** declares members without instance fields. Classes, structs, and records can **implement** multiple interfaces. An interface is a Common Language Runtime (CLR) contract: the runtime knows which types implement it, and you can cast to the interface type. This is how a worker depends on `IBus` without taking a concrete `RabbitBus` type — composition with a type-checked seam.

entries.plainDefinition: A named contract of members (methods, properties, events) that implementing types must provide. No instance fields allowed.
entries.example: `interface IBus { Task PublishAsync(string key, CancellationToken ct); }`

entries.plainDefinition: An interface member with a body, added in C# 8. Existing implementers get the default without recompiling.
entries.example: `void Log(string msg) => Console.WriteLine(msg);` inside an interface.

entries.plainDefinition: Implementing an interface member with the interface name prefix. The member is hidden from the class's public surface unless you cast to the interface.
Wrapping a value type (struct) in a heap object when it is stored as an interface or object reference.
entries.example: A struct implementing `IEquatable<T>` boxes when cast to `IEquatable<T>`.

blocks.text: Interfaces are the primary way to define replaceable dependencies in .NET services. Your worker takes `IAttemptStore`, not `SqlAttemptStore`. Tests inject an in-memory fake. Production injects the real database adapter. Default Interface Methods (DIM) let you evolve a public interface by adding a member with a default body — existing implementers compile without changes. Explicit implementation disambiguates when two interfaces declare the same member name.

blocks.title: Struct-to-interface boxing
blocks.body: When a struct implements an interface and you store it as the interface type, the CLR boxes it — copies the struct onto the heap wrapped in an object. For hot paths with small value types, keep the concrete struct type instead of the interface reference.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Declare the interface
items.body: Define the contract with method and property signatures. No fields, no constructors.

items.title: Implement on a class or struct
items.body: Add `: IMyInterface` to the type declaration and provide every member.

items.title: Depend on the interface, not the concrete type
items.body: Constructor parameters and fields use `IBus`, not `RabbitBus`. The composition root wires the concrete type.

items.title: Cast when you need the interface view
items.body: For explicit implementations, call through the interface type: `((IBus)bus).PublishAsync(key, ct)`.

snippet.label: Default interface method plus explicit implementation
snippet.explanation: Line 4: DIM provides a convenience overload with a default body. Line 9: explicit implementation keeps `PublishAsync` off `RabbitBus`'s public surface. Line 16: the DIM overload is visible through the `IBus` reference and calls the explicit core method.

snippet.label: Multiple interfaces on one worker
snippet.explanation: Line 11: one class implements two interfaces — no extra base class needed. Line 13: `IAttemptHandler` behavior. Line 16: `IHealthCheck` behavior. The host can register this type for both roles.

snippet.label: Struct implementing an interface — boxing awareness
snippet.explanation: Line 5: struct implements the interface. Line 10: storing as `ICacheKey` boxes the struct onto the heap. Line 11: keeping the concrete struct type avoids boxing. In hot cache-key paths, prefer the struct type directly.

snippet.label: Explicit implementation for two interfaces with the same member
snippet.explanation: Explicit implementation disambiguates colliding member names and hides them from the class public API. Callers depend on the interface type — the same pattern as injecting IBus instead of RabbitBus in production.

blocks.title: Interfaces across languages
rows: Structural — any matching object satisfies the type
CLR metadata; casts and is checks work
DIM with bodies on the interface (C# 8)
No runtime default; optional properties in TS only

blocks.title: Fat interfaces (Interface Segregation Principle violation)
blocks.body: An `IWorkerBase` with twenty methods forces every implementer to provide fakes for methods it never uses. Split into small, focused interfaces: `IAttemptStore`, `IBus`, `IClock`. Callers depend only on what they need.

blocks.title: Forgetting DIM visibility rules
blocks.body: A default interface method is only callable through the interface type unless the implementing class redeclares it. If you add a DIM and callers use the concrete type, they will not see the new member until they cast or the class redeclares it.

blocks.text: Interfaces are nominal CLR contracts stored in metadata — unlike TypeScript structural typing. Each implemented interface adds an interface mapping entry the runtime uses for casts and `is` checks. Default Interface Methods (DIM) ship a body on the interface itself; the CLR resolves the most specific override (class beats DIM). Explicit interface implementation keeps versioning seams clean: you can add IAuditableV2 members without polluting the public class surface. Struct-to-interface conversion always boxes unless you use generics constrained to the struct type. How to prove it in production: dotnet-counters or a profiler showing GC Gen0 spikes when a hot Redis key path stores `ICacheKey` instead of `RedisKey`, or BenchmarkDotNet comparing struct direct versus interface reference.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Test fakes implement only what callers need
More types to register in DI
Add members without recompiling all implementers
Only visible through interface unless redeclared
Disambiguate collisions; hide from public API

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Treating C# interfaces like TypeScript structural types — C# requires `implements` and runtime casts fail on wrong CLR types. Saying DIM replaces abstract base classes for shared state — interfaces still cannot have instance fields. Ignoring struct boxing on hot paths — storing IEquatable<T> instead of T boxes value types. Strong answer: nominal contracts, many per class, DIM for evolution, explicit for collisions, watch struct boxing in cache and message paths.

interviewTakeaways: Many interfaces, one class base; interfaces are nominal CLR contracts, not structural duck typing.
DIM evolves contracts; explicit implementation disambiguates and hides members from the class surface.
Struct-to-interface conversion boxes — keep concrete struct types on hot Redis and cache-key paths.

60s: Interfaces are CLR contracts. Many per class. DIM adds default bodies visible through the interface type. Explicit implementation hides colliding members. Struct cast to interface boxes — measure on hot paths.
Follow-up: when would you choose explicit implementation over a public method on the class?
commonPitfalls: Treating interfaces as structural like TypeScript — saying any object with matching members satisfies the contract gets rejected in C# interviews.
Strong answer: nominal typing; must declare implements; runtime is checks use CLR metadata.
Fat interfaces that force fake implementations of twenty methods never used by the caller.
Forgetting a DIM is only visible through the interface type unless redeclared on the class.

jsTsCorrelations.note: TypeScript interfaces are structural and erased. A matching object literal satisfies them. C# interfaces are nominal and require an implements clause.
JavaScript will call obj.publish() if it exists. C# will not compile a call without a type that has the member; interface casts fail at runtime if the object is the wrong CLR type.
